events.title: The Search for Silicon Valley’s Most Powerful Woman
events.summary: Mira Murati was trying to speak. Women swished around in evening gowns, men in tuxes. Giant piles of carved meat rested like sleeping babies on banquet tables draped in linens as red as a handmaid’s robe. Bartenders served up a cocktail named Zero to One, a nod to the philosophy of Peter Thiel. It was a recent Saturday night in a converted church in San Francisco, and the Foundation for American Innovation, a center-right think tank, was hosting a black-tie affair to hype the new religion of AI. Murati, the founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab , was talking about the history of revolutions to a crowd of more than 350 people. The Albanian-born executive had for several years kept a relatively low profile as a VP and then CTO of OpenAI before participating in an unsuccessful coup against Sam Altman and then launching her own $12 billion AI startup. Now, with chatter bouncing off the church walls, Murati’s efforts to get her points across were about as successful as that coup: No one seemed to be listening. The woman interviewing Murati asked more than once for people to stop talking or take their conversations outside. I whispered to the friend sitting next to me that this was the second time in a week that I’d seen a woman getting drowned out. She sighed. Both of us were there to actually hear what Murati had to say. I tried to restrain myself from what I said next, but I sensed my friend was holding back too. “Her hair is amazing, though,” I hissed. “Oh my God, I know,” she replied immediately. Murati’s hair has achieved AGI. Her jaw cuts glass. Soon after, President Donald Trump’s top science adviser, Michael Kratsios, took the stage. The crowd quieted down. We are all part of the problem. Over the past three months, I’ve been asking anyone and everyone about the most powerful women in Silicon Valley, a club to which Murati clearly belongs. Ask who the most powerful man in tech is and many quickly say “Elon.” Or “Jensen.” Or “Sam.” Wait a beat and you might hear the name of a billionaire VC whose financial capital has been broadly and ruthlessly deployed to advance an agenda, like “Peter” or “Marc.” Ask who the most powerful woman is, and most people respond with a thoughtful pause. A thinking-face emoji. “Gwynne?” “ Lisa ?” “Daniela, maybe?” An astute observer of the Valley might posit that the most powerful woman has to jet-set between SV and DC, like Ruth Porat, the president and chief investment officer of Google, or Dina Powell McCormick, Meta’s president and vice chair. WIRED’s top editor—a woman—said at one point, “Isn’t it obviously Gwynne Shotwell?” Then a Silicon Valley CEO told me that whenever she mentions the SpaceX president and chief operating officer, her friends say “Gwynne who?” Some people seemed allergic to my question. They don’t view tech as gendered, they told me, or didn’t have much to say. Who cares? Just put your head down and do the work. Still, the question provoked reactions. My conversations—which took place on the phone and Zoom, in boardrooms, in San Francisco coffee shops, in a Palo Alto home where my source dozed off on the couch—produced a wealth of options, ranging from founders and CEOs to venture capitalists and philanthropic ex-wives. Some of those women, both CEOs and those who call bullshit on CEOs, spoke to me at length. Nobody wants to talk about women in tech anymore—not even women in tech . Is that progress? I realized that the real question is not who is most powerful, but why this question is still, in 2026, so difficult to answer. What’s missing from their lives or résumés? Why is there no woman Elon? Why don’t we have our own all-powerful heroine or supervillainess? In June, a friend and former Slack executive suggested to me that power in Silicon Valley contains multitudes of capital—financial, intellectual, political, and social or cultural. We agreed that the mononymous men score high in all categories. Their influence has been stunning, alarming even, in its contagion. They write blog posts that are referenced for decades. They dox people with a single post on X. They sway elections. They deliver sermons. They are asked to sign a woman’s breasts at a trade show in Taiwan, like some ’80s hair-metal frontman. They suggest that a young woman trying to save the planet is the antichrist. Does any woman in tech come close to achieving this cult of personality, to spreading the seeds of their capital in this way? There is no “Time to Build” manifesto that the women of the Valley are rallying around. The last time women in tech had a manifesto, things didn’t go as planned. On a recent drive to Lake Tahoe, I downloaded the audiobook of Sheryl Sandberg’s Lean In . I’d read the book when it came out in 2013, and I wanted to see how its ideas had aged. By the third chapter I had heard enough. My brief listen reminded me, though, of why the book had been influential for nearly a decade.

events.title: Nvidia’s free AI model could push the UAE closer to the U.S.
events.summary: The Emirates owns the machines but rents the intelligence. Nvidia’s next free AI model could change that. Nvidia’s chips are driving the United Arab Emirates’ rise as an artificial-intelligence power. Next on offer is free software, a model built to rival China’s best. Last month, Nvidia spent $7 billion to buy a stake in U.S. coding startup Poolside and license the tools it uses to build AI models. The new model is due by the end of the year for anyone to download for free, and it is aimed at buyers already running Nvidia hardware, Marc Einstein, an analyst at Counterpoint Research, told Rest of World . Few countries fit that description better than the UAE, whose flagship data center will run on 400,000 Nvidia chips . For years the UAE positioned itself as neutral ground between the U.S. and China, buying chips from the former and, until recently, equipment from the latter. It built its own free model, Falcon, to avoid relying on imported software. That neutrality has been fading since G42, the state-backed AI company, cut its Chinese ties to win Nvidia’s chips. It would narrow further if the country also opts for the new model. “The last missing piece was the model layer,” Mohammed Soliman, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a foreign-policy think tank in Washington, told Rest of World . “Nvidia already owns the chips. Now it is scaling the factory that produces the models that run on those chips, and it is releasing them as open weights.” The two institutions leading the UAE’s AI push each have their own view on whether to build sovereign AI models from scratch or lean on existing technology from other companies. The Technology Innovation Institute, the government lab behind Falcon, insists on building its own models from the ground up, while G42, which runs the UAE’s AI infrastructure, has aligned itself with Nvidia’s push for free models. The value is not limited to the models we ultimately produce, but it lies in mastering the underlying technology and retaining control.” Hakim Hacid, chief researcher, Technology Innovation Institute “As a model-building lab, we believe that maintaining diversity in AI perspectives, and preserving full technological sovereignty, requires a strong, homegrown foundation,” Hakim Hacid, TII’s chief researcher, told Rest of World . “The value is not limited to the models we ultimately produce, but it lies in mastering the underlying technology and retaining control across the entire AI stack.” G42 did not answer Rest of World ’s questions about whether it would use Nvidia’s model. The company has been an early supporter of Nvidia’s push to give away powerful models. In July, Nvidia formed an alliance around the argument that countries need AI models they can inspect and control, and G42 joined immediately, becoming the only Gulf company to do so. “Frontier open models are an essential part of that future, alongside frontier closed models, with security, trust and sovereign control designed in from the start rather than bolted on later,” G42’s CEO, Peng Xiao, wrote on X at the time. Building on someone else’s model need not mean giving up control, Soliman said. Sovereignty in AI is a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing choice, he said. “Sovereignty was never about inventing the foundational model from scratch,” Soliman said. “It is about the model’s weights, how you fine-tune the data, and, most importantly at this stage, your ability to serve these models to users in the UAE and other markets.” The U.S. government approved sales of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to the UAE after G42 sold its stakes in Chinese technology companies two years ago. In July, it placed the UAE in the group of countries it treats as its closest technology allies. The software running on those chips is mostly rented from U.S. companies, which decide what the models may do and who may use them. Falcon was meant to be the exception. TII built it in 2023 as a free alternative to models from the U.S. and China, and it ranked first this year on Counterpoint’s index of state-backed models. Saudi Arabia, which is competing with the UAE to become the region’s AI hub, has taken a different route. Humain, the state AI company, is cleared to buy tens of thousands of Nvidia chips, and introduced an Arabic model this month that it had commissioned from a Chinese lab. A year earlier, it had launched one it said was built from scratch in the kingdom. “It shows there’s little full-stack lock-in: The Saudis are using Chinese AI models to build their own models, while using U.S. chips to develop and run them,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow at the think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Rest of World . “These states have strong incentives to hedge and will continue to do so for as long as they can.” Nvidia has its own reasons for wanting countries to take the upcoming model, expected to be called Nemotron 4. events.title: Inside a low-key House Democratic leadership fight
events.summary: The News House Democrats are fighting over the pecking order in their extended leadership hierarchy as they hope to win the majority. In recent days, allies of both Reps. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., and Ted Lieu, D-Calif., have laid claim to the fourth-ranking slot in the majority as they look to potentially convert their current titles (assistant Democratic leader and caucus vice chair, respectively), into the equivalent roles in the majority (assistant speaker and caucus chair). Top Democrats are publicly staying above the fray. “We have a great team,” said Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., “Everybody has a role to play, and everybody’s valued.” A person close to leadership noted that Minority Whip Katherine Clark was considered the fourth-ranking Democrat when she was the assistant speaker under Nancy Pelosi. A senior political adviser to House Democratic leadership said the “tradition continues as it has been.” Democrats’ internal rules lay out an election order, though the House’s website lists Lieu above Neguse. “I’m laser-focused on flipping the House. American families are struggling with high costs, and democracy is literally on the line,” Lieu said in a statement. Know More It’s not the first time there’s been ambiguity in the hierarchy. The last occupant of Neguse’s job, Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., created some murkiness when he stepped down from his top leadership position and into the assistant leader job by taking himself out of the line of leadership succession. There’s not much practical implication of the leadership hierarchy besides dictating the speaking order at press conferences, but it can give lawmakers bragging rights or set them up for future jobs. Members of the current top trio — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Clark, and Aguilar — all previously served in the rung of leadership below Pelosi’s top tier, though the order of those roles didn’t make a difference for the jobs they hold now. Additional Democrats are still maneuvering for other jobs in the leadership chain. Lawmakers in the mix for the DCCC chair include Reps. Lizzie Fletcher, D-Texas, Brad Schneider, D-Ill., Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., and Steven Horsford, D-Nev. Two are squaring off for vice chair: Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill. At least three Democrats are vying to join two open spots on the party messaging arm: Reps. Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., Sarah McBride, D-Del., and Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif. The top Education and Workforce Committee Democrat, Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, is also facing challenges, with Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-Conn., actively running and Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, D-Ore., weighing a bid .

events.title: ‘This pushes the boundaries’: White House helped Pentagon explain the legality of its equity deals
events.summary: The Scoop One month before the Pentagon announced its first equity stake in a company, its top lawyer asked the White House to explain why the deal wouldn’t break the law. The White House budget office responded with a previously unreported legal opinion, reviewed by Semafor, that provides a crucial look at how the Trump administration justified one of its most controversial deployments of taxpayer money in the private sector. A multibillion-dollar agreement with rare earth firm MP Materials is exempt from the law that bars the executive branch from spending taxpayer money without Congress, Office of Management and Budget General Counsel Mark Paoletta argued in June 2025, because it was “necessary to avoid an imminent threat to human life and government property.” The Pentagon would be relying on authorities provided by the Defense Production Act and annual defense legislation from 2017, Paoletta continued, as well as Article II of the Constitution. The deal would be the latest in a “venerable tradition of presidential obligations in advance of appropriation,” he concluded, stretching back to 1792. While the Pentagon went on to strike more deals for equity in companies — including its most recent agreement with Venezuelan oil company North American Blue Energy Partners — former Pentagon officials told Semafor they were skeptical of Paoletta’s reasoning. For the moment, the Defense Department’s investments are operating in a legal morass that lawmakers in both parties see as unsustainable. The Senate Armed Services Committee wants Congress to pass its already-advancing plan to give the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital explicit legal authority for its equity stakes, a spokesperson for Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., told Semafor. OSC, which was created to issue loans, has been involved in a majority of the equity agreements. Wicker “believes that an appropriately scoped equity investment authority is important for continued positive work in restoring a free market for critical minerals,” the spokesperson added. “But he also believes the department must regularize the process surrounding equity-based deals and increase its transparency with the Congress to render this approach sustainable over the long term.” One former Pentagon official said that the law barring taxpayer expenditures without Congress, known as the Antideficiency Act, was “one of the hurdles we thought was going to be insurmountable” for the MP Materials deal. Another former OSC official said they were “surprised that the current team has discovered the authority to do this under the Defense Production Act,” adding that “laws can be elastic, but elasticity snaps at some point.” “I think this pushes the boundaries,” the official continued. OSC’s role in the MP Materials deal was limited to a $150 million loan under its statute, a Pentagon spokesperson told Semafor, while the Pentagon’s Acquisitions and Sustainment Unit made the $400 million equity investment using authorities granted by the Defense Production Act. The Senate Armed Services panel has requested briefings from the OSC on the Pentagon’s legal authority to take equity, people familiar with the talks said. events.title: Why the Senate won’t vote to repeal new Canada tariffs
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s new Canada tariffs are infuriating Democrats and annoying some Republicans — but Congress is unlikely to vote on them before the election. Trump’s use of a nearly century-old law to impose the levies takes away individual senators’ ability to force such a vote on the Senate floor like they did with the previous set of Canada tariffs, which were imposed under a different statute, noted Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. And that means Republican committee chairmen and leaders control any effort to curtail them — not rank-and-file Democrats. “The other tariff statutes don’t have this privileged motion that a single senator can force a vote on the floor,” Kaine said. He added that tariff opponents can write bills to block the tariffs, but under Republicans, “they get sent to a committee” and “the committee bottles it up.” Instead, Democrats are eyeing pre-election Iran war votes. Know More Just last year, individual senators used their powers under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to vote to block earlier Canada tariffs, but there’s no such option this time around. It’s no secret that Democrats would like to see Republicans have to take as many tough votes as possible right up until the election, although it’s also possible some GOP incumbents would vote against the tariffs given the option, knowing full well that Trump would veto any effort to undercut his tariff power. Democrats are still on track to force votes to restrain Trump’s war powers on Iran, having teed up a resolution written by Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., Kaine said. Those votes are increasingly challenging for some GOP senators as the war drags on. “We’re trying to do one every week. Sometimes the schedule makes it hard, but our goal is to do one every week until war’s over,” Kaine said. Democrats are surprisingly bullish on succeeding with their Iran war votes; they’d need five Republicans to vote with them if Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., continues to break with his party in order to get enough GOP support to get a simple majority. But there are scheduling battles playing out behind the scenes. The Senate is still working on the bipartisan college sports bill for the foreseeable future, and Republicans want to hold votes on regulatory rollbacks in exchange for another vote on the Iran war. There’s likely to be some horse-trading to get those votes over the next two weeks.

events.title: France’s ‘school of happy globalization’ refocuses on security
events.summary: The News It was a scary weekend in European capitals, where leaders fretted about Russia testing NATO’s limits and grappled with a threatened drawdown of American troops in Europe. French President Emanuel Macron delivered a briefing to the candidates running to succeed him so disturbing that even the far-right National Rally’s leaders emerged denouncing Russian hybrid attacks. The looming question is whether European leaders, institutions, and citizens can pivot swiftly enough so that the bloc can use its economic heft to take responsibility for its own security. One institution is testing that: Sciences Po, the training ground for French and other European policy elites, has sharply redirected its resources to the moment. This fall, it launched a new Centre for Global Security and Governance and expanded its defense and intelligence offerings, the school’s president, Luis Vassy, told Semafor. “We had been the school of happy globalization,” he said in a phone interview from Paris on Sunday. “We need to readjust the mindset of future European elites to a world that is going to be more competitive, more brutal.” “That doesn’t mean we should dissolve our value system, but if we believe it’s a value system that is worth defending, that has some consequences in terms of the way we should act,” he said. Sciences Po, which also recently launched a climate school to meet the other looming crisis, had long lacked the sort of security-minded focus on “international relations” present at big American universities — take, for example, Johns Hopkins SAIS and Columbia University SIPA. The field “in its US shape is seen as a right-wing domain, because it is states, it’s power, it’s conflict,” Vassy said. “If you look at issues more from the bottom-up, you look more into social trends, the oppressive nature of the state, et cetera.” But his students have already begun to pivot for the new moment: Defense and security majors in the existing policy school have increased 30% per year for the last three years, he said, and the school of international affairs is launching new concentrations in defense and intelligence to meet the rising demand. This reflects a new consensus that, however far Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth take their current campaign, a new era has begun. “If India can be independent from a defense standpoint there’s no reason Europeans shouldn’t,” said Vassy, a former French diplomat in Washington and chief of staff to the Foreign Ministry. “It’s simply not reasonable to have your whole security depending on a foreign actor.” Sciences Po’s graduates typically supply about three-quarters of the enrollees at the training academy for French leaders known as ENA. Barring a cultural revolution, its current students will more or less be running the country from about 2045 to 2070. Ben’s view Even as European leaders press forward to centralize the bloc’s economy and invest in its shared security, the rising politics in Germany and France are pulling those nations in the opposite direction. The radical AfD in Germany and moderating National Rally in France are both focused on ending immigration and enjoy support from voters wary of escalating conflict with Russia. The longer-term trend, though, is clear. Sciences Po’s turn reflects a European assumption that, whatever happens in the US elections in 2026 and 2028, the American security umbrella is receding over the long term. “I worked in the foreign ministry where we could happily lecture the rest of the world. This is completely outside their worldview,” said Vassy. Instead, the new classes are “extremely conscious about the challenges. They have not been educated like you and me in a world where the West was the unique center of power.” Room for Disagreement “The European Union is a vehicle for economic cooperation. It is a peace project, not a war project,” Hugo Bromley wrote in Foreign Affairs in March , arguing that an attempt to build a common European defense front would turn into a domestic political disaster. Notable Vassy laid out his views recently in Grand Continent : “We have moved from with our ideas, our values, and our strengths, to ,” he wrote, according to a translation from French.

events.title: Watch: The New Supreme Court
events.summary: Source image: Bryan Dozier/NurPhoto via AP The Supreme Court continues to make consequential rulings in the shadows. I analyzed tens of thousands of case files from the court’s online archives , parsing through filings to separate simple requests for deadline extensions from challenges to long-established constitutional rights. I discovered that in the term that ended in 2025, the justices issued more substantive decisions on their emergency docket than in cases argued in open court. Experts told me this was likely the first time this has happened in the court’s modern history.  Representatives from the Supreme Court did not respond to my questions.  Since I reported that story in July, more major rulings have been made on the emergency docket, often called the “shadow docket,” where justices rarely hear arguments and often issue unsigned orders that don’t explain how they arrived at their decisions or even how they voted. These decisions are continuing to come down even after the court began its summer recess. For example: On Aug. 31, the court allowed construction to continue on a ballroom at the White House. Requests like this one from the president are a big reason why the number of cases being handled on the court’s shadow docket has been so high. On Sept. 10, a decision blocked Missouri from using a redrawn congressional map crafted by the state’s Republican-controlled legislature. The legislature had redrawn the maps at President Donald Trump’s request — part of a string of middecade redistricting efforts that could determine control of Congress. Like most shadow docket decisions, no opinion was issued and there is no record of how the justices voted. On Sept. 14, the court stopped the U.S. Postal Service from imposing new regulations on voting by mail that the Trump administration was seeking to impose. Less than a month earlier , the court had said it was too early for states to challenge those regulations. The court rulings came just weeks before most states begin sending out ballots by mail. Though experts told me rulings on the shadow docket have generally enabled Trump, he has not won them all. The USPS ruling, for one, has not pleased the president. Last week, in a post on Truth Social, the social media website he owns, Trump criticized the justices he nominated, writing that they “are not the people I interviewed to serve.”  “It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history,” Trump wrote. Every decision the court has made since July has been on its shadow docket. That will remain the case until the court starts its new term on Oct. 5.  Watch our explainer to learn more about what I uncovered and how the shadow docket works. The post Watch: The New Supreme Court appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
events.summary: Germany's car crisis: Will the 35-hour workweek survive? German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights. Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs , intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles . Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs. The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country. Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027. Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition. The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on? Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum. "In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000." Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added. Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals. Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a report published by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay. The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s. It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over." Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours. Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union , said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough. The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced. IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector. Can longer working hours save jobs? The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said. The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%. "We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined. Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions. On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added. "Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel. How can Germany's auto industry recover? Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems. "Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel. He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes. "German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel. At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure. Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production?
